\section[alegrarse]{alegrarse — to be glad}

\label{lesson:ES-C487-alegrarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the aspirin, then the Spanish for the vaccine.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: alegrarse}
\textbf{alegrarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to be glad\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Me alegro de verte.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am glad to see you.}
\end{quote}

It goes with \emph{de}: \emph{alegrarse de algo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{alegrarse} is built on \emph{alegre}, \textquotedblleft{}cheerful\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{alacer}, \textquotedblleft{}lively, brisk\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), through a spoken form \emph{*alecris} — inherited: the \emph{-c-} became \emph{-g-}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{alegrarse}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{alegrarse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{alegrarse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the aspirin, then the Spanish for the vaccine, then say \emph{alegrarse} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does alegrarse mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To be glad\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[enfadarse]{enfadarse — to get angry}

\label{lesson:ES-C487-enfadarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the vaccine, then the Spanish for to be glad.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: enfadarse}
\textbf{enfadarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to get angry\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi hermana se enfada si llego tarde.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My sister gets angry if I arrive late.}
\end{quote}

In much of Latin America people say \emph{enojarse}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{enfadarse} probably comes from Galician-Portuguese \emph{enfadar}, \textquotedblleft{}to weary, to annoy\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{fado}, \textquotedblleft{}fate\textquotedblright{}, Latin \emph{fatum}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{enfadarse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{enfadarse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the vaccine, then the Spanish for to be glad, then say \emph{enfadarse} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[preocuparse]{preocuparse — to worry}

\label{lesson:ES-C487-preocuparse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to be glad, then the Spanish for to get angry.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: preocuparse}
\textbf{preocuparse} — \textquotedblleft{}to worry\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No te preocupes, todo va bien.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Do not worry, everything is fine.}
\end{quote}

It goes with \emph{por}: \emph{preocuparse por alguien}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{preocupar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{praeoccupare}, \textquotedblleft{}to seize beforehand\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1): \emph{prae-}, \textquotedblleft{}before\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{occupare}, \textquotedblleft{}to take hold of\textquotedblright{}. A worry is a thought that has taken hold of you first. A learned word: the \emph{-p-} between vowels was kept, where speech made \emph{saber} from \emph{sapere}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to be glad, then the Spanish for to get angry, then say \emph{preocuparse} again

\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]

\section[divertirse]{divertirse — to have fun, to enjoy yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C487-divertirse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to worry, then the Spanish for to relax.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: divertirse}
\textbf{divertirse} — \textquotedblleft{}to have fun, to enjoy yourself\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Nos divertimos mucho en la fiesta.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We had a lot of fun at the party.}
\end{quote}

The e breaks into ie under stress: \emph{me divierto}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{divertir} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{divertere}, \textquotedblleft{}to turn aside\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1): \emph{di-}, \textquotedblleft{}apart\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{vertere}, \textquotedblleft{}to turn\textquotedblright{}. Fun is a turning aside from cares.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}
